artwork.title: The Raft of the Medusa
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Shonagon, 2025, via Wikimedia Commons · Public Domain

lessons.title: Hope without a goddess

n1.text: This canvas is almost a storey high and more than seven metres wide. Bodies lie at the bottom left. At the top right, a man waves a cloth at something far away.

q1.text: Which part pulls you in first?

b1a.text: He's at the top of a pyramid of bodies: a Black man waving a cloth toward a ship you can barely see.

b1b.text: Bodies lying, hanging, propped up. Some may be dead; others exhausted or unconscious. It's hard to tell them apart, and that difficulty is the weight of the painting.

b1c.text: A huge sea, a huge sky, and on the horizon a ship so small it's unsettling. You can see every muscle on the raft. The rescuers may not see them at all.

n2.text: This really happened. In 1816 the French navy ship Méduse ran aground on the way to Senegal. People were put on a raft, the tow was cut, and they were abandoned. Only fifteen survived.

voice.speaker: gericault
voice.text: I met two of the survivors, Corréard and Savigny. Their published account had made the wreck a scandal.

q2.text: You're Géricault. Which moment do you paint?

choices.label: The moment they spot a ship

b2a.text: Dramatic, but he skipped it. He chose the moment they spot a tiny ship and start waving, before anyone knows if they'll be saved.

voice.speaker: gericault
voice.text: The wreck was only the beginning. I wanted the moment they see the ship, before anyone knows if they'll be saved.

b2b.text: He didn't show the rescue as done. He chose the moment just before: a tiny ship, men waving, and no way to tell if help is coming.

b2c.text: That's his choice. A tiny ship on the horizon, men starting to wave, and no way to tell yet whether they'll be saved.

voice.speaker: gericault
voice.text: Yes. The ship is there, tiny. Nobody on the raft knows yet whether it will come.

n3.text: That uncertainty is the point: the gap between seeing rescue and being rescued. Now trace the shapes. Bodies climb from the bottom left toward the waving man, forming a pyramid.

q3.text: What forms a second triangle beside that pyramid?

b3a.text: Right. Mast, ropes and sail make a second triangle. Side by side, the two make the raft feel held together and pulled apart at once.

b3b.text: The waves do another job: they make this last scrap of floor feel unsafe. The second triangle is the mast, ropes and sail.

n4.text: Two triangles: one of bodies rising, one of mast and sail. Low means close to death; high means trying to be seen. Now look at those bodies again.

q4.text: The real survivors were starving. Why do these bodies look so strong?

b4a.text: Yes. Muscular, twisting nudes at this scale belong to the art of heroes and saints; the Louvre links them to Michelangelo. It gave nameless victims public weight.

b4b.text: He did use survivors' accounts. But the waving man was posed by a professional model, Joseph, not a survivor. And the heroic strength is deliberate.

voice.speaker: gericault
voice.text: I listened to survivors, yes. But the man waving was posed by Joseph, a professional model.

n5.text: Heroic bodies, borrowed from paintings of saints and heroes, given to ordinary people from the news. And now look at the colour: the whole painting is very dark.

q5.text: Is all that darkness Géricault's choice?

b5a.text: Not all of it. As early as 1881, the Louvre worried that the painting kept darkening, and linked it to bituminous materials and the oil medium.

b5b.text: Right. Louvre records from 1881 already worried about the darkening, linking it to bituminous materials and the oil medium. The concern led to a reproduction print.

n6.text: Nobody commissioned it. Géricault made it for the 1819 Salon, possibly hoping the state would buy; it entered the royal collection only after his death in 1824. There's no goddess here. Survivors have to lift themselves and wave.

voice.speaker: gericault
voice.text: Nobody asked me for it. I showed it at the 1819 Salon under a quieter title: Scene of a Shipwreck.

lessons.takeaway: Géricault painted the moment hope appears but isn't yet real. Two triangles, heroic bodies, and a darkness that is partly time.
